name: Mark-Recapture Population Calculator
seoDesc: Estimate how many animals are in a population from two visits: mark a sample, release them, then count how many marked individuals turn up in a second sample.
summary:
Estimate how many animals are in a population from two visits: mark a sample, release them, then count how many marked individuals turn up in a second sample. It returns population estimate, chapman estimate, share marked in the second sample and 95% confidence, lower, and the panel shows all of them at once.

The Lincoln–Petersen estimator is the simple proportion, and the Chapman correction makes it usable when samples are small. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mark-Recapture Population
sections.html:
N ≈ (M × C) ÷ R. Chapman: N = (M+1)(C+1)/(R+1) − 1

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
Manimals marked and released in the first sampleanimals
Canimals caught in the second sampleanimals
Rof those, how many carry a markanimals

sections.title: How do I use the Mark-Recapture Population?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter how many animals you marked and released (M).
  2. Enter the size of the second sample (C) and how many of them were already marked (R).
  3. Read the estimate, the Chapman-corrected value and the confidence interval.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: marked in the first sample of 80, total caught in the second sample of 100, of those, already marked of 20.

Substituting them into the formula gives population estimate of 400, chapman estimate of 388.57, share marked in the second sample of 20%, 95% confidence, lower of 263.88, 95% confidence, upper of 513.27.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
R ≥ 20Reliablethe estimate is stable and the interval is tight
R 5 – 20Usable with careuse the Chapman correction; expect a wide interval
R under 5Unreliablethe interval will be enormous — mark more animals

  • The method assumes a closed population: no births, deaths, immigration or emigration between the two samples, and marks that do not fall off or change behaviour.

  • The Lincoln–Petersen estimate is biased high when R is small — it cannot even return a value below M plus the unmarked animals you saw. The Chapman correction exists for exactly this.

  • The confidence interval depends almost entirely on R. Twelve recaptures is the practical minimum for a number you would publish.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Comparing samples taken in different seasons, when the population is not closed.
  • Marking only conspicuous animals, which are then more likely to be caught again.
  • Reporting the point estimate without the interval — it can easily be ±40%.

faq.a: A closed population, equal catchability of marked and unmarked animals, and marks that are neither lost nor harmful.
The plain Lincoln–Petersen estimator is biased upward for small samples; Chapman's version is close to unbiased.

faq.q: How many recaptures do I need?
faq.a: At least twenty for a useful interval, and never fewer than five for a number worth reporting.

faq.q: What does the Mark-Recapture Population actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns population estimate, chapman estimate, share marked in the second sample and 95% confidence, lower. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
